title: The three colors — red, white, black (6.4)
hook: look at a flame: the red is heat, the white is water, the black is food, and the 'fire' itself turns out to be a name
tomorrow: food, water, heat become mind, breath, speech

segments.voice: Yesterday: sat, Being alone, one without a second. Your line was it thought: let me be many. Heat, then water, then food. What did you notice growing from one into many? Day three hundred forty-two.

Light a match and look closely at the flame. It isn't one color. There's a reddish glow, a bright whitish part, and a dark edge where the wick or the stick is burning down. Usually it's just fire, blown out before it reaches your fingers. Uddalaka, teaching his son, looks at the same flame and sees the whole creation story from yesterday, still going on, right there in the colors.
screen: `LIGHT A MATCH.` → `NOT ONE COLOR.` → `THE CREATION STORY, STILL GOING.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Being became three things: heat, water and food. Now Uddalaka says Being entered into them with the living self, and gave them name and form, and wove each one together with the other two, so that everything is a braid of three. Then he points to a fire. The red color of fire is the form of heat. The white color is the form of water. The black color is the form of food, of earth. And then he says something startling: so the fireness of fire has gone. The change is only a name, a matter of words. The truth is the three colors. You've heard that phrase before. It's the clay line from two days ago, word for word, except now the pot is a flame. He does the same with the sun, the moon and lightning. Red, white, black, in each. Sun-ness, moon-ness, lightning-ness: names. The three are what's there. Then he adds something about the old teachers. The great householders of old, he says, knew this, and so they said: nobody can now tell us anything we haven't heard or thought or known. Whenever they saw something red, they knew it as heat. White, as water. Black, as food. The point isn't really chemistry. Nobody's claiming this is how a modern lab would describe a flame. The point is a way of seeing. Behind the bright, separate things of the world, Uddalaka sees a few simple strands, and behind those strands, the one Being they came from. Look behind the colors, and the world gets simpler, not smaller.
screen: `EVERYTHING IS A BRAID OF THREE.` · `RED IS HEAT, WHITE WATER, BLACK FOOD.` · `THE FIRENESS OF FIRE HAS GONE.` · `THE OLD HOUSEHOLDERS KNEW.` · then, large: `THE TRUTH IS THE THREE COLORS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice looks behind the colors. If you can, look at a candle, a lamp, or a sunlit patch of wall; if not, close your eyes and picture a flame. Breathe. Notice the different colors in it. As you find each one, give it Uddalaka's meaning: red, heat. White, water. Dark, food. Three strands, one flame. Then close your eyes and rest with the afterglow, in whatever is there behind it. The bell holds the time.
Trivrit, threefold, braided of three. Red for heat, white for water, black for food: Uddalaka's way of seeing every fire, sun and moon this way.
Your line: behind the colors. Today, look at one beautiful thing, a sunset, a face, a dish of food, and ask what simple things it's made of. Day three hundred forty-two.

screen: `DAY 342 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FOOD, WATER, HEAT BECOME MIND.`

howItsDone: The idea that everything is woven of a few basic strands runs through later Hindu thought, including the three gunas of Samkhya and the Gita; some scholars see Uddalaka's three colors as an early forerunner of these ideas, though the link is debated.

fork.setup: you're one of the great householders of old. you've understood the three colors. someone offers to teach you something new about the world. what do you say?
options: nobody can now tell us anything we haven't heard or known.
fork.reveal: the text says the old householders said just that: knowing the three, they could see what anything was made of.

original.note: Sanskrit trivṛt: threefold, braided of three. Being made each element trivṛt.

trapdoor: what you thought: an ancient guess about why fire has colors.
what it means: a way of seeing. everything is braided of heat, water and food, and behind them, one Being.
what a scholar hears: Chandogya 6.3–6.4, the trivritkarana or 'making threefold'; it repeats 6.1.4's clay formula with fire, sun, moon and lightning.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'most of us just see fire' cut; practice changed so it no longer repeats day 340's name-it-then-let-the-name-go move (now traces each color to heat, water, food).
Hook's description of a match flame (reddish glow, white part, dark edge) is illustrative only; confirm it isn't presented as the text's claim.
'Fire' in 6.4.1 is agni; the three forms rūpa of tejas, ap, anna. Confirm wording.

howItsDone links to the gunas as a later development; confirm this is a fair, non-anachronistic note. Reviewer softened it from 'Vedanta teachers read the three colors as an early form of this' to 'some scholars see ... a forerunner ... debated'; Shankara's own link is to trivrtkarana/pancikarana, not the gunas.

Teach says the fire formula repeats the clay line of 6.1.4 'word for word'; it is the same formula (vacarambhanam vikaro namadheyam ... ity eva satyam) with fire in place of clay. Confirm the claim is fair.
